episode_title: A Career in Transition: From Oil and Gas to Clean Tech

real_qa.q: What was Jane Woodward's role at ARCO and how did it shape her investment perspective on natural gas?
real_qa.r: At ARCO from 1982 to 1985, Woodward became an expert on where natural gas reserves existed across U.S. sedimentary basins. ARCO paid her to identify the leading experts on conventional gas reserves and hydrocarbon source rocks, which later became shale gas plays. This three-year training directly informed her conviction to invest in natural gas when she co-founded MAP Energy, recognizing an innovation wave driven by changes in technology, markets, and policy including the Clean Air Act and combined cycle gas turbines.
real_qa.requete: Jane Woodward ARCO natural gas shale plays

real_qa.q: When did MAP Energy begin investing in wind energy and why did the timing work despite early failures?
real_qa.r: MAP Energy entered wind investing after observing that the gaseous regions of the U.S.—Texas and Oklahoma—were also among the windiest. Woodward had been teaching about wind since 1991 and taking students to Altamont Pass. The company benefited from inherited projects from Kenetech's bankruptcy portfolio around 30 projects in development, and they recognized that major utilities were beginning to pursue wind easements in areas where MAP already held relationships through mineral rights transactions.
real_qa.requete: MAP Energy wind investment Kenetech projects

real_qa.q: What was Kenetech's business model and why did it fail in the early wind industry?
real_qa.r: Kenetech attempted to be 'the Standard Oil of wind' by vertically integrating every part of the wind business: manufacturing wind turbines, owning and operating wind farms, and operating globally. The company came in too early, doing too much too fast across too many markets simultaneously, and ultimately went bankrupt. However, some of the last people to survive Kenetech's bankruptcy inherited a portfolio of approximately 30 wind projects in development.
real_qa.requete: Kenetech wind turbines bankruptcy vertical integration

real_qa.q: Why did wind investors in 2003-2004 initially resist allocating capital to wind energy funds?
real_qa.r: When MAP Energy's investors were approached in 2003 with a 2004 fund proposal requesting 10% allocation to wind exposure, investors reacted with extreme skepticism. Many investors trusted the proposal only because Woodward taught at Stanford, expressing fears that 'our money is going to be blown in the wind.' Some investors had the reaction that she was proposing investment in nuclear waste, so terrified were they of committing capital to wind technology at that time.
real_qa.requete: MAP Energy 2003 2004 wind fund 10 percent allocation

real_qa.q: How did horizontal drilling technology transform natural gas and oil extraction compared to vertical drilling?
real_qa.r: Horizontal drilling allowed operators to penetrate up to a mile of reservoir versus only 100 feet with vertical wells, dramatically reducing both risk and cost. It enabled drilling fewer wells while achieving radically lower surface impact. T. Boone Pickens explained that while hydraulic fracturing had been used for over 60 years in vertical wells, the innovation was applying it horizontally—like sending a straw sideways underground instead of straight down, compared to the medical analogy of angioplasty versus open-heart surgery.
real_qa.requete: horizontal drilling natural gas vertical wells mile reservoir

guest.bio_context: Jane Woodward began her career as an exploration geologist with ARCO, then worked as a petroleum engineering consultant before co-founding MAP Energy, where she built an investment practice from traditional energy into renewables. She has taught energy and environmental courses at Stanford University since 1991, and currently leads Woven Earth Ventures, which invests in early-stage climate technologies.
